summary:
Maryland sits inside the United States federal document regime, which is the sharpest document risk for any trans visitor to the country. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, so new passports are issued as M or F on the supporting documents submitted; passports already carrying an X marker remain valid to expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU is in litigation with the State Department, and the Supreme Court has allowed the department's changed treatment of trans passports to proceed. A visitor's passport can therefore mismatch the traveller's presentation, and there is no state override available inside Maryland.

Entry adds a second exposure that applies at the border rather than inside the state. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code SWS25. The same announcement states that declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. Airport screening carries a related involuntary-disclosure risk: the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guidance describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening type matching one's presentation.

Against that federal backdrop, Maryland is among the more protective states for trans residents. The state's Trans Health Equity Act, sponsored in the Maryland House of Delegates by Del. Anne Kaiser, D-Montgomery, extends Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming treatment; its legislative passage in 2024 is tracked in firm commentary as the measure moved through the Senate. Coverage of gender-affirming care is one of the substantive protective features a trans visitor encounters in Maryland, and Maryland's document rules and its treatment of trans health care stand apart from the restriction wave visible in other states.

Facility access is where the national picture diverges sharply by state. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with some jurisdictions criminalising trans bathroom use in certain circumstances, while twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia carry no such ban. Maryland is not among the jurisdictions identified in that reporting as enforcing a facility restriction. Enforcement elsewhere is not theoretical: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, identified by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. Visitors entering states with such bans, including through transit, face a different regime.

Protective law in Maryland has not prevented violence against trans residents. On 11 September 2026 a 27-year-old Black trans woman, Sophie Lee, was found shot in Baltimore's Charles Village and died, the second Black trans woman shot to death in Baltimore within ten weeks. A July 2026 analysis plotting recorded anti-trans incidents against each state's law score places Maryland in the 'Safest States' band, at a law score of 23.5 with 11.1 recorded incidents, and notes that Louisiana records both the worst law score, 24.7, and the highest recorded incident count, 11.6, a comparison the analysis uses to argue that protective law floors do not by themselves determine incident counts.

Monitoring and external guidance point the same way. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving national trends; Maryland is not identified in that assessment among the flagged states. Multiple foreign governments have issued their own advisories: at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, those advisories following detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Detention carries its own exposure. Federal policy on housing transgender detainees and prisoners moved sharply between 2015 and 2018: a January 2015 ICE memo directed that transgender immigration detainees be housed according to gender identity, and 2016 Department of Justice guidelines forbade corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units on birth anatomy alone. The Federal Bureau of Prisons revised its Transgender Offender Manual in 2018, deleting the sentence that the Transgender Executive Council 'will recommend housing by gender identity when appropriate' and replacing it with case-by-case placement in which biological sex is the initial determination and gender identity is used only in rare cases.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 comparison plots recorded anti-trans incidents against state law scores and finds that the two do not move together. Maryland sits in the 'Safest States' band at a law score of 23.5 with 11.1 recorded incidents; Louisiana carries both the worst law score, 24.7, and the highest recorded count, 11.6. A visitor weighing Maryland against another state on the strength of its statutes alone should treat the incident data as a separate signal.

Foreign advisories are themselves a form of evidence about the current risk. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and those changes followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues. Where an allied government warns its own trans nationals, the underlying concern is documentation and entry, which is precisely the exposure a Maryland visitor carries.

The federal prisoner-housing record is relevant background even where it has no local equivalent. The 2015 ICE memo on gender-identity housing for immigration detainees and the 2016 DOJ corrections guidelines were both displaced in practice by the Bureau of Prisons' 2018 revision, which places biological sex as the initial determination and limits gender identity to rare cases. Detention risk therefore exists at the federal level regardless of state policy.
localsOnly:
Maryland's Trans Health Equity Act was carried in the Maryland House of Delegates by Del. Anne Kaiser, D-Montgomery, with firm commentary tracking the measure's path through the Maryland Senate. The Act extends Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming treatment, and that coverage is a resident-facing benefit rather than a traveller provision, though it shapes the care environment a long-stay visitor may encounter.

No Maryland-specific placement policy, special unit, or named case governing the housing of transgender prisoners is recorded in the sources reviewed. Residents held in Maryland's corrections system are covered by the federal framework described above rather than by a state rule documented here.

Account from trans women held in men's facilities describes the V-coding practice of assigning trans women to aggressive cisgender male cellmates, characterised as a central part of a trans woman's sentence, and reports that trans women who physically resist sexual assault are often charged with assault, held in solitary confinement, and have the charge used to extend their sentence and deny parole. A 2021 California study found that 69% of surveyed trans women prisoners reported being made to perform unwanted sexual acts, 58.5% reported violent sexual assault, and 88% reported a marriage-like relationship. These figures are drawn from a California study and are not Maryland data.
outOfScopeNotes:
Maryland's own identity-document rules are not established in the sources reviewed here. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions; whether and how Maryland appears on that map is not stated in the material available, so the state's marker-change procedure remains unresolved for this dossier.

The Trans Health Equity Act's effective date and the size of the covered trans population are not stated in the sources used for this pass. The firm-blog tracker documents the 2024 passage and the sponsor line and follows the Senate path; any specific effective date or coverage estimate should be verified against the enacted text and state health department reporting before publication.

The national bathroom-ban count covering nine states and one territory is stated without a list of those jurisdictions in the material reviewed, so whether Maryland falls inside or outside that count is inferred from its absence from the named jurisdictions and should be checked against the underlying tally. Similarly, the 13 July 2026 risk assessment names Idaho as the fourth do-not-travel state but does not enumerate all four in the material reviewed; Maryland's absence from the flagged group is read from the same analysis that places Maryland in the 'Safest States' band.

Incident counts are drawn from a single July 2026 analysis without a stated methodology for what qualifies as a recorded anti-trans incident, so cross-state comparisons, including Maryland's 11.1 against Louisiana's 11.6, should be treated as indicative rather than precise.
